content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper enables text conditioned modulation of the “style” of a stylegan like image generator in a feed forward fashion rather than relying on a costly per “style” optimization as it was the case for previous SOTA works (Style-GAN). In practice given a couple of keywords “source” and “target” the proposed model predicts an edit direction in the “w+” latent space of the generative model that allows the “target” property to emerge. The method is trained on 100 different keywords and is shown to: perform on par or better than “StyleGAN-NADA” (the previous SOTA) fine tuned on each target word independently. The method also partially generalizes to unseen words and to different generator architectures (i.e., EG3D and StyleSWIN). The evaluation is conducted in terms of a user study.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

+ The proposed method achieves competitive or better results than the previous SOTA without requiring a costly fine-tuning for each possible “couple” of keywords. This cuts down inference time and memory requirements significantly.

+ I liked the proposed Identity preservation loss (section 3.3). It provides a neat and clean way of enforcing some kind of disentangled edits in the w+ latent space by forcing modification only along one direction of the considered vocabulary.

+ The proposed method seems to generalize with no major modification to other style-based GANs like EG3D and StyleSwin. To the best of my knowledge, this has not been shown before. I found it interesting to see that these latent spaces exhibit properties similar to the styleGAN ones.

## Weaknesses

a) The method section of the paper can be improved both in organization and content. 
  * Regarding organization, I would suggest moving section 3.5 after 3.2 and before 3.3, such that the main loss is presented before talking about the additional regularization introduced. 
  * Regarding content, after reading the paper I still have some doubts that don’t allow me to fully understand the paper, mainly: is the generator GAN frozen during training? How are the training keywords selected? Is there any enforcing of disjoint concepts being picked as keywords? 

b) The main advantage of the method is to not need a costly retraining for each pair of keywords which was the key for the previous SOTA. However it’s not clear to me how a frozen generative network can be manipulated to this extent simply by moving in fixed directions in the latent space. One of the contributions of StyleGAN nada was showing that indeed that was not the case, and for going out of training distribution there was the need to modify the weights of the generator. Can the authors comment on this more explicitly in the paper? If my understanding is correct and the paper does not modify the weights of the generator this work basically confutes the findings of StyleGAN-NADA.

c) The computed transformation on the w+ space to apply the “target” transformation has two main drawbacks in this formulations: first it requires a corresponding “source” keyword to use as starting point (and the author did not comment much on how this was picked for the experiments), second it applies the same transformation independently of the latent code z being sampled. While this seems to work for global representations like the one shown in the qualitative example it could be a limiting factor for transformations that require some form of understanding of the image being modified. The current method basically learn a set of edits to go from “source” to “target” irrespective of the actual image content encoded in “w”. Note that these however are also drawbacks of the main competitors StyleGAN-NADA.

d) d) The main quantitative result of the paper is based on a human evaluation but there’s no additional details on how the evaluation was conducted and how many people were involved. This exposes the paper to lack of reproducibility and potential biases in the way the human evaluation was conducted.

e) Lack of details on how the method was applied to EG3D and StyleSwin. For example EG3D has two latent spaces both conditioned by the original z, one controlling the multiplane generator and one controlling the super resolution network, on which one did the authors operate? On the concatenation of all of them?

f) There’s no discussion on how/if the method can be successfully applied with inversion methods to edit real images. Without this component the method is not particularly useful as it can be used only to edit random sampled latent codes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity

Clarity of the method can be improved, the main idea and the results are clearly presented, but many details are missing or not discussed in the paper. See weakness (a)-(b) for more details. 

## Quality

The results achieved by the model are quite good for in-domain modifications and compositions of them (Fig. 3 - Fig. 4), however generalization to out-of-vocabulary terms seems still subpar (Fig. 8), even tough this is more like an exploration of what the model could do rather than a quality claim on these samples. Nevertheless the paper does improve over the SOTA for in-domain samples.

## Novelty

The work belongs to a quite underrepresented field of study and does introduce significant novelties with respect to previous works

## Reproducibility

I feel like some details are missing to make the work reproducible (see weakness a-b-d). The authors claim that the code will be made public making at least the retraining part of the work reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: I liked the main idea of the paper and the results are quite impressive for edits on the training vocabulary, however right now I cannot suggest acceptance of the paper for two main reasons: firstly many details are missing in the paper and should be clarified (weaknesses a-b-e), second there’s no example of applying the proposed method to inverted real images (weakness f) which would be the real use case of this technology.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a framework for adapting pre-trained GAN generators to new domains defined by a set of keywords (in natural language) using a pre-trained CLIP model, without training on new images or fine-tuning the GAN generator. The authors do so by training a latent mapper (LAMDA) in order to map directions in the CLIP text space into directions in the GAN's latent space. The authors state that the proposed method has been jointly trained on a 100 keywords set, but the results reported in the manuscript are on around 10 of them. The main contributions of the proposed method are: a) that adaptation is achieved without fine-tuning the pre-trained GAN generator and b) that training is being conducted jointly for the given set of keywords taking into considerations the relative position of the training keywords in the CLIP embedding space. Limited qualitative comparisons with one SOTA method (i.e., StyleGAN-NADA) show potentially better (but subjective) visual results, while quantitative comparison is very limited (only in terms of LPIPS) and insufficiently explained.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---
The paper's main strength lies on the fact that the incorporated pre-trained GAN generator is not fine-tuned during training. The only trainable module of the proposed framework is a fully-connected (FC) mapper network that maps directions from the CLIP text space to the GAN's latent space. It is very interesting that the achieved results (even only after carefully tuning the hyperparameters) are obtained without modifying the generator. Additionally, the joint optimisation of a set of keywords is another strong point.


Weaknesses
---
My main point of criticism concerns the technical novelty of the propose framework and the experimental evaluation scheme reported in the paper.

First, from a technical point of view, the paper does not propose anything novel, that has not been proposed/used in prior similar works.
 - More specifically, the main adopted loss is similar to that of StyleGAN-NADA, a work closely related to the proposed one.
 - The additional so-called ID losses (L_ID and L_magnitude) are not clear at all regarding how they impose the preservation of ID. Specifically, they do so by penalizing the mapper based on the difference between the keyword similarities before and after translation. In my opinion, this so-called ID loss (L_ID) serves a role that a similar contrastive loss would do possibly more effectively. In any case, it is not clear to me why ID is encouraged to be preserved by this loss -- likewise, the same holds for L_magnitude. Instead of using the aforementioned ID losses, it would make more sense to experiment with ArcFace [1], which is the standard loss used by related literature in order to impose ID preservation.
 - An ablation study on the significance of each loss term is required to show whether the ID losses help in preserving ID or to show how directional margin helps.
 - It is not clear (since it is inconsistent throughout the manuscript) which GAN latent space is being used (W or W+). It is important to clarify this, and in the case of W+ to clarify on which (out of the 18 layers in StyleGAN2@FFHQ1024, for instance) layers and how the mapper learns to map CLIP text directions onto W+ directions. Working on a subset of W+ layers (e.g., on the first 8) has been shown to produce better results in terms of ID preservation and disentanglement (e.g., see StyleCLIP). Additionally, the recent Style Space S [2] has been shown to be extremely disentangled, and a discussion, even better experimentation, on this latent space would strengthen the claims of the paper.

Second, the experimental evaluation of the proposed framework is limited.
 - Out of the 100 keywords used in training, the paper reports results only on a few of them (around 10). The reported keywords, in my opinion, are not all extremely useful (e.g., "cthulu art", "minions"), or at least it is not clear to me why they are. It would make sense to report results on more keywords, possibly easier to evaluate both quantitatively and quantitatively, such as facial expressions or facial attributes (e.g., CelebA's attributes), that can be evaluated by appropriate pre-trained classifiers/detectors.
 - The qualitative evaluation scheme is not clear and limited. Specifically, the user study process needs to be clarified (how many users, whether results' origin is hidden from the users, etc).
 - Comparison to SOTA could be more extensive. Since, the proposed method does not modify the GAN's generator during training, it could be compared to StyleCLIP or other recent text-driven generation methods (which also do not fine-tune the generator). Moreover, a more thorough discussion on the reasons why StyleGAN-NADA cannot be adapted to the multi-keyword framework would improve and strengthen the paper (if this is true). I would expect that a method that fine-tunes the GAN generator (such as StyleGAN-NADA) would be expected to achieve better results. Is this not-feasible? It is not clear why in the case of StyleGAN2, at least.
 - Instead of experimenting with more complex GAN architectures (where fine-tuning might be impractical), I think that exploring other style-based (StyleGAN-XL [3]) or non-style-based (e.g., ProgGAN [4]) would improve the paper.

Finally, I felt that in quite a few instances the paper makes very bold statements that are not supported theoretically or empirically:
 - "[...] LAMDA produces excellent results [...]" -- this is a bold statement regarding very limited results (a few images manipulated using a few keywords). In addition, the selected keywords might not be as interesting/useful as the authors state (e.g., "Cthulu art", "minions").
 - (Sect. 3.4)"[Directional margin] serves two benefits: it increases disentanglement between learned directions, and it allows for a small amount of variation for each keyword" -- these claims are not proven in the paper.
 - (Sect. 4.4) "[...] this proves that the network is not overfitting [...]" -- it is bold to use the term "proves" here, since there is no empirical or theoretical data to support it.

Minor comments:
The manuscript can be improved significantly in terms of use of language and structure. The structure and the presentation can be improved. For instance, the related work section should focus more on works that are closer to the proposed method than in more general areas (like GANs as generative networks). More specifically, the paper would benefit from a more thorough discussion on the differences between the proposed method and StyleGAN-NADA, StyleCLIP, and other recent text-driven manipulation methods.


References

[1] Deng, Jiankang, et al. "Arcface: Additive angular margin loss for deep face recognition." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2019.
[2] Wu, Zongze, Dani Lischinski, and Eli Shechtman. "Stylespace analysis: Disentangled controls for stylegan image generation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021. 
[3] Sauer, Axel, Katja Schwarz, and Andreas Geiger. "Stylegan-xl: Scaling stylegan to large diverse datasets." ACM SIGGRAPH 2022 Conference Proceedings. 2022.
[4] Karras, Tero, et al. "Progressive growing of gans for improved quality, stability, and variation." arXiv preprint arXiv:1710.10196 (2017).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This work appears to be original. The manuscript can significantly be improved in terms of quality and clarity. Bold statements should be removed in the cases where what is claimed is not proved empirically or theoretically. Attention should be paid in consistency (e.g., stating clearly what is the GAN latent space used each time, if it's W+, which layers, etc). Reproducibility at this point is limited since the authors do not provide information of the architecture of the proposed latent mapper (FC), specifically the output dimension which is dependent to which GAN latent space is being used, but they authors state the code will be made publicly available.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a way of learning to adapt a pre-trained GAN generator (without fine-tuning its parameters) into domains defined by a set of keywords. This is interesting, but both the technical content an the experimental evaluation are limited (see weaknesses above), failing to show that the claimed merits of the method are true.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces CLIP models to find the editable directions in the latent space of generative adversarial networks. The performance is generally good.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
1. The proposed method is simple but seems to be effective.
2. This paper is well organized and achieves promising results on face images.

### Weaknesses
1. I wonder how many attributes can you success to edit. It seems that this method requires a large number of data to discover the directions that can be edited?
2. As the key word is photo, why the experiments are only performed on face images (human or cat face), how about other images, such as natural scene?
3. Which factor affects the diversity of the proposed method?
4. The results deeply depends on the pre-trained CLIP model, the performance can be affected by the CLIP model.
5. How the interrelations between different keywords benefit the model?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall, this paper has good writing quality. However, some experimental details are not properly clarified, as mentioned in the weakness part.
content.summary_of_the_review: As CLIP model has been widely applied in many related works, although this paper achieves relatively considerable results, the novelty is some what limited.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an approach that can adapt a GAN to new domains as defined by keywords.  The authors motivate this by recent findings that support that the latent space of GANs is - to a large extent - disentangled in terms of visual attributes.  The method builds on StyleGAN-NADA, and claims to improve in terms of speedup by facilitating training on a large number of keywords simultaneously rather than fine-tuning a network.   In principle, instead of that, when training the authors randomly sample words out of the keyword list and thus train the mapper between the directional clip loss and the direction in the GAN latent space.  New changes can then be incorporated additively.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[S] as presented, the method does indeed appear faster than stylegan-nada
[S] it is a smart idea, connecting two recent observations in the generative models area
[W] The paper puts forward bold claims (better quality , generalization to unseen attributes etc). Experiments are lacking, in my opinion, to support these claims well.  In particular:
- there is only one method that the approach is compared against - and that is only evinced by one figure (Figure 3) and one table, with only one subject.
- The authors claim that their work is better on 'difficult' keywords: what does that mean in practice? attributes that are not well supported in the data?
- Figure 8 on unseen attributes is presented as acceptable, however I`m not sure if qualitatively one can tell.  Clearly there is a change of identity in many of the results, albeit having some similarities.  Not sure that this makes sense to be used as a claim in the paper - even mentioned in the abstract.
- Although the authors claim that stylegan-nada has difficulties with longer sentences - this paper does not show any such results either.
[W]  Since the main competitor, stylegan-nada, requires fine-tuning a network - could the relatively bad results in Figure 3 be due to fine-tuning/training parametrization and setting?  The style-gan-nada has shown better results than the ones presented in this paper, and with only 1 subject/figure this is hard to tell.
[W] there is an incremental element to this work
[W] Ablation studies are necessary to indicate the value of individual components
minor points:
-Figure 2 could be made more informative
-how the lambda mapper is trained should be hinted at earlier in the text
-typos
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- the paper has an incremental elements, building directly ona previous method 
- the merit of the idea is to do away with fine-tuning a net, but to learn a mapper to the latent W+ space
- some parts of the paper - inc methodology could be made more clear
content.summary_of_the_review: This work builds directly on stylegan2-nada and essentially learns a mapper network to W space instead of fine-tuning a net for a keyword.  This has implications in terms of speed, but the paper lacks in terms of sufficient experimental results to support these claims well.  please see detailed points above also
